title: What do you think? — giving opinions
goal: Give an opinion, agree and disagree at the level of certainty you actually mean — from a confident *menurut saya* to a cautious *sepertinya* — and do it the Indonesian way, where open disagreement is softened before it is spoken.
bekal: open an opinion with *menurut saya*, *bagi saya*, *saya kira* or *sepertinya* and know which is stronger
agree and disagree politely: *saya sependapat*, *ada benarnya juga*, *saya kurang setuju*
follow and take part in a *musyawarah*, the village way of reaching a decision

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Musyawarah tiket masuk
dialogs.intro: A Tuesday evening in early April, at the village hall. Pak Harun has called a meeting to decide how much visitors should pay to enter the desa wisata. Bu Ratna, Sarah and Pak Darto, the farmer Sarah interviewed for the survey, are among those present.

lines.speaker: Harun:
lines.text: Bapak-Ibu, malam ini kita membahas tiket masuk desa wisata. Silakan sampaikan pendapat.
lines.id: Ladies and gentlemen, tonight we're discussing the entrance ticket for the tourist village. Please give your views.
lines.literal: sirs-madams, night this we discuss ticket enter village tourism. please convey opinion.

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Menurut saya, dua puluh ribu per orang itu wajar, Pak.
lines.id: In my view, twenty thousand a head is reasonable.
lines.literal: according-to me, two ten thousand per person that reasonable, sir.

lines.speaker: Darto:
lines.text: Bagi saya itu kemahalan, Bu. Tamu dari Magelang sendiri bisa kabur.
lines.id: For me that's too expensive. Even visitors from Magelang itself would run a mile.
lines.literal: for me that too-expensive, madam. guest from Magelang self can run-off.

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Tapi uangnya kan untuk kebersihan dan perawatan jalan, Pak Darto.
lines.id: But the money goes on keeping things clean and maintaining the roads.
lines.literal: but money-the [kan] for cleanliness and maintenance road, Mr Darto.

lines.text: Mbak Sarah, bagaimana pendapat Mbak dari sisi pengunjung?
lines.id: Sarah, what's your view from the visitor's side?

lines.text: Saya kira tamu mau membayar, asal jelas apa yang mereka dapat.
lines.id: I think visitors will pay, as long as it's clear what they get.
lines.literal: I guess guest want pay, provided clear what that they get.

lines.speaker: Darto:
lines.text: Maksudnya bagaimana, Mbak?
lines.id: What do you mean?
lines.literal: meaning-its how, Miss?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Misalnya, tiketnya sudah termasuk teh, pemandu, dan peta desa.
lines.id: For example, the ticket already includes tea, a guide and a village map.
lines.literal: for-example, ticket-the already included tea, guide, and map village.

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Nah, saya sependapat dengan Mbak Sarah.
lines.id: There you go, I agree with Sarah.
lines.literal: there, I same-opinion with Miss Sarah.

lines.speaker: Darto:
lines.text: Kalau boleh jujur, saya masih kurang setuju. Warga sekitar jangan disamakan dengan turis.
lines.id: To be honest, I'm still not quite convinced. Local people shouldn't be treated the same as tourists.
lines.literal: if may honest, I still less agree. resident around don't be-equated with tourist.

lines.speaker: Harun:
lines.text: Ada benarnya juga. Bagaimana kalau warga Kabupaten Magelang cukup membayar lima ribu?

lines.literal: exist truth-its also. how if resident regency Magelang enough pay five thousand?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Sepertinya itu jalan tengah yang adil, Pak.
lines.id: That sounds like a fair compromise.
lines.literal: it-seems that road middle that fair, sir.

lines.speaker: Darto:
lines.text: Kalau begitu, saya bisa menerima.
lines.id: In that case, I can accept it.
lines.literal: if like-that, I can accept.

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Saya juga setuju, Pak Kades.
lines.id: I agree too, Mr Village Head.
lines.literal: I also agree, Mr Village-Head.

lines.speaker: Harun:
lines.text: Baik. Jadi kita sepakati: dua puluh ribu untuk umum, lima ribu untuk warga Magelang.
lines.id: Good. So we agree: twenty thousand for the general public, five thousand for Magelang residents.
lines.literal: good. so we agree-on: two ten thousand for public, five thousand for resident Magelang.

notes: **Musyawarah** is deliberation until everyone can live with the result (*mufakat*, consensus). A vote is the last resort, not the first. That is why Pak Harun keeps looking for a middle way instead of counting hands — and why the meeting takes as long as it takes.

**Menurut saya vs bagi saya.** *Menurut saya* (“according to me”) states a view about the world. *Bagi saya* (“for me”) says how something looks from your own position — Pak Darto is thinking of his own neighbours' wallets. Both are neutral and polite.
**Kemahalan** — the *ke-…-an* “too” from Unit 4: too expensive for the purpose. Pak Darto could have said *terlalu mahal*; *kemahalan* sounds more personal and more rural, which suits him.

**Saya kira** — literally “I guess”. It is the modest way to say “I think” and is safer than *saya pikir*, which is extremely common but is sometimes criticised as a translation of English “I think”. In writing, prefer *saya kira* or *menurut saya*.

**Kalau boleh jujur, saya masih kurang setuju.** Two cushions in one sentence: “if I may be honest” asks permission to disagree, and *kurang setuju* (“less than agreeing”) is how disagreement is normally voiced in public. A flat *saya tidak setuju* at a village meeting would sound confrontational.
**Pak Kades** is short for *Kepala Desa*, the elected village head. Indonesian loves these clipped titles: *Pak RT*, *Pak Camat*, *Bu Lurah* — you address the office rather than the person's name.

grammars.title: Opinion openers, from confident to cautious
body: How you open an opinion tells people how firmly you hold it. The list runs roughly from the most certain down to the most tentative.
after: *Menurut* also works with any person: *menurut Pak Darto* (“according to Pak Darto”), *menurut data UGM*, *menurutmu?* (“what do you think?”). It is the single most useful word in this unit.
💬 In chat you will see *menurutku* and *kayaknya* everywhere; *kayak* is the spoken form of *seperti*.

grammars.title: Agreeing and disagreeing without a fight
body: Indonesian has a generous middle ground between yes and no, and polite speakers live in it. Use the soft rows at meetings and with anyone older or senior.

head: Indonesian
English
Note
rows: Forgive me, I see it differently.

after: A common pattern is **agree first, then disagree**: *Betul juga, Bu, tapi…* The first half costs nothing and makes the second half acceptable.
⚠️ *Saya tidak setuju* is grammatically perfect and fine among friends. At a meeting with elders it can sound like a challenge. When in doubt, go one step softer than you would in English.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Beda pendapat dengan Bu Lestari
dialogs.intro: Two days later, a video call. Dr. Lestari has read the minutes of the village meeting and has a different priority in mind.

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Mbak Sarah, saya sudah membaca notulen musyawarah. Menurut hemat saya, yang lebih mendesak adalah pembatasan jumlah pengunjung.
lines.id: Sarah, I've read the minutes. In my humble view, the more urgent matter is limiting visitor numbers.
lines.literal: Miss Sarah, I already read minutes deliberation. according-to consideration my, which more urgent is limitation number visitor.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Maksud Ibu, kuota harian?
lines.id: You mean a daily quota?
lines.literal: meaning madam, quota daily?

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Tepat. Data kami menunjukkan bahwa jalan desa tidak mampu menampung lebih dari tiga ratus orang per hari.
lines.id: Exactly. Our data show that the village roads can't take more than three hundred people a day.
lines.literal: exact. data our show that road village not able accommodate more than three hundred person per day.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Saya paham, Bu. Tapi kalau boleh jujur, sekarang pengunjungnya baru lima puluh orang seminggu.
lines.id: I understand. But to be honest, at the moment we only get fifty visitors a week.
lines.literal: I understand, madam. but if may honest, now visitors-the only-just five ten person one-week.

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Karena itu aturannya harus dibuat sekarang, sebelum masalahnya muncul.
lines.id: That's exactly why the rules have to be made now, before the problem appears.
lines.literal: because that rule-the must be-made now, before problem-the appear.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Ada benarnya juga. Namun saya khawatir warga merasa dibatasi terlalu cepat.
lines.id: You have a point. But I'm worried people will feel restricted too soon.
lines.literal: exist truth-its also. however I worried residents feel be-limited too fast.

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Pendapat Mbak masuk akal. Bagaimana kalau kuotanya diberlakukan mulai tahun depan?
lines.id: That's a fair point. What if the quota came into force from next year?
lines.literal: opinion Miss enter mind. how if quota-the be-made-valid start year front?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Saya setuju, asal warga diajak bicara lebih dulu.
lines.id: I agree, as long as people are consulted first.
lines.literal: I agree, provided residents be-invited talk more first.

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Tentu. Kita sampaikan di musyawarah berikutnya.
lines.id: Of course. We'll raise it at the next village meeting.
lines.literal: certainly. we convey at deliberation next.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Terima kasih, Bu. Enak sekali berbeda pendapat dengan Ibu.
lines.id: Thank you. It's a real pleasure disagreeing with you.
lines.literal: thank you, madam. pleasant very differ opinion with madam.

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Sama-sama, Mbak. Berbeda pendapat itu sehat.
lines.id: Likewise. Disagreement is healthy.
lines.literal: same-same, Miss. differ opinion that healthy.

notes: **Menurut hemat saya** — *hemat* normally means “thrifty”, but here it is an old word for “careful consideration”. The phrase is a modest, academic “in my view”, heard in seminars, editorials and from people like Dr. Lestari.

**Data kami menunjukkan bahwa…** — the academic habit of letting evidence speak instead of the person. *Bahwa* (“that”) is almost compulsory in this register after *menunjukkan*, *berpendapat* and *mengatakan*; in speech it often disappears.
**Pengunjungnya baru lima puluh** — *baru* here is “only (so far)”, with a feeling that more will come (Unit 5). *Hanya lima puluh* would sound like a complaint; *baru* sounds like a beginning.
**Namun** is the formal “however”. Sarah switches to it because she is disagreeing with a senior academic. In chat with Yoga she would say *tapi*. Unit 9 looks at all these contrast words.
**Masuk akal** — “enters the mind”, i.e. makes sense, is reasonable. *Nggak masuk akal!* is “that's absurd!”, and you will hear it about prices, traffic and politics.

**Diberlakukan** — from *berlaku* (to be valid, in force). The *ber-* verb keeps its prefix and takes *me-…-kan* around it: *memberlakukan*, to put into force, passive *diberlakukan*. You will meet it in every news story about a new regulation.

grammars.title: The academic and formal register of opinion
body: Dr. Lestari's opinions sound more objective because she wraps them in fixed formal phrases. You need to recognise them in seminars, reports and the news, and use a few in formal writing.

head: Formal phrase
Everyday equivalent
English
rows: I am of the opinion that…
I don't entirely share that view.

after: Formal opinions tend to remove *saya* altogether and use a passive: *Perlu dipertimbangkan bahwa…* (“it should be considered that…”). This is not coldness; it is how Indonesian academic writing sounds.
Mix registers carefully. A formal opener followed by *nggak* and *kayaknya* sounds odd — rather like opening with “I would respectfully submit” and ending with “innit”.

sections.title: Asking other people what they think

blocks.text: Asking for opinions is part of being polite in Indonesia, especially if you are the one with power in the room. A chair who never asks *Bagaimana, Bapak-Ibu?* is considered rude, however efficient.

*Masukan* (literally “input”) is the standard word for feedback or suggestions. *Kritik dan saran* is the formula at the end of every presentation: *Kritik dan saran sangat kami harapkan* — “we welcome criticism and suggestions”.

blocks.title: Softening an opinion even further
items: *agak*: *Menurut saya harganya agak mahal.* — a bit expensive, not outrageous.
*mungkin*: *Mungkin sebaiknya kita tunggu dulu.* — perhaps we should wait.
*sebaiknya*: “it would be better to”, the polite way to recommend anything.
Turn it into a question: *Bagaimana kalau tiketnya lima belas ribu saja?*

sections.title: Musyawarah untuk mufakat: how a village decides

blocks.text: The phrase *musyawarah untuk mufakat* — deliberation towards consensus — is in the national ideology and on the walls of village halls. In practice it means everyone speaks, the chair sums up, and a compromise is announced as if it had been obvious all along.

blocks.title: Reading the room
items: Silence is not agreement; it often means someone is unhappy but will not say so in public.
Elders usually speak last, and their view often closes the matter.
If you disagree strongly, a private word afterwards may achieve more than a speech.

blocks.text: For a foreigner the safest role at a *musyawarah* is the one Sarah takes: speak when asked, offer a practical suggestion rather than a verdict, and let the village own the decision. An idea that the chair can present as the meeting's own is far more likely to be adopted.
Cover the Indonesian column, read the English, and rebuild each sentence from memory.
